title: Al, the Underworld Dweller
summary: A demonic being who lives in the depths of the earth, luring the living underground with promises of treasure, because in Georgia the earth itself hungers.
full_text:
Al is the lord of the underworld. He lives beneath the mountains of Georgia, in caverns so deep no lamp can light them. He is massive. His body is black. His eyes are red. His voice is the sound of rock splitting.

Al does not come to the surface often. When he does, he comes for a reason. He comes for people.

Al calls to miners. He calls to men who dig into the earth for gold and silver. He whispers to them. He tells them where the richest veins are. He tells them where the deepest gold lies.

The miners follow the voice. They dig deeper. They dig past the safe layers. They dig into the dark. The earth closes behind them. The tunnel collapses. The miners do not return.

Al takes the miners underground. He keeps them as servants. They mine for him. They dig his caverns. They carry his treasure. They never see the sun again.

Al also takes women. He appears to them at night. He appears as a handsome man. He seduces them. He takes them underground. They become his brides. They live in the dark. They forget the light.

The only protection against Al is iron. An iron knife placed under the pillow keeps Al away. An iron nail driven into the doorframe keeps Al out. Iron burns Al. Iron is the one thing the underworld cannot contain.

The miners of Chiatura carry iron. They tie iron nails to their belts. They hang iron above the mine entrance. They pray to God before they descend. They do not pray to Al. To pray to Al is to belong to Al.

Al waits. He is patient. The earth is deep. The gold is deep. The miners will come.
moral: The deeper you dig, the closer you get to what waits below.
source: Georgian oral tradition, documented by Ekvtime Takaishvili

title: Amirani, the Chained Hero
summary: A Titan-like hero who defied the gods and was chained to a mountain for eternity, his chains binding him until the day a greater hero comes to free him.
full_text:
Amirani was a hero. He was stronger than any man. He was braver than any warrior. He challenged the gods. He fought them. He won.

The gods were angry. They could not kill Amirani. He was too strong. So they chained him. They chained him to the highest peak of the Caucasus. They bound his hands. They bound his feet. They bound his neck.

The chains are made of the same metal as the stars. They cannot be broken. They cannot be rusted. They cannot be cut.

Amirani hangs on the mountain. His body is exposed. The sun burns him by day. The frost freezes him by night. The eagles tear at his flesh. The flesh grows back. The eagles return. The cycle continues.

Amirani does not die. He does not scream. He waits. He waits for the hero who will come to free him. The prophecy says the hero will be born in Georgia. The hero will be stronger than Amirani. The hero will break the chains.

When the chains break, the world will change. The gods will fall. The mountains will move. The sea will dry up. A new age will begin.

The people of Georgia tell the story of Amirani to their children. They point to the mountains. They say, "There. That is where Amirani hangs. Look at the snow on the peak. That is the frost that freezes him."

The children look. They see the mountain. They see the snow. They wonder about the hero who waits.

Amirani does not wonder. He knows. The hero is coming. The chains will break. The world will change.
moral: Some heroes are measured not by their victories, but by their endurance.
source: Georgian national mythology, Mesrop Mashtots manuscripts

title: Ali, the Mountain Demon
summary: A monstrous demon who dwells in the high mountains, stealing livestock and children, because in Georgia the peaks belong to things older than faith.
full_text:
Ali is not Al. Ali is different. Al lives underground. Ali lives in the mountains. Al tempts. Ali takes.

Ali is a demon. He is large, larger than a man. His body is covered in hair. His eyes are burning. He has horns. He has hooves. He smells of sulfur.

Ali lives in the high mountains, above the tree line, where the rocks are bare and the wind never stops. He has a den. The den is filled with the bones of animals. The bones of sheep. The bones of goats. The bones of children.

Ali steals livestock. He comes down from the mountain at night. He opens the pen. He takes the best sheep. He carries them up the mountain. The shepherd wakes in the morning. The best sheep are gone.

Ali also takes children. He appears to them when they are playing alone in the fields. He appears as a beautiful horse. He lets the child ride him. The child rides. The horse runs. The horse runs up the mountain. The child does not return.

The only protection against Ali is prayer. A prayer said before entering the mountains keeps Ali away. A cross drawn on the door of the sheep pen keeps Ali out. The name of God spoken aloud burns Ali's ears.

But prayer is not always enough. Ali is strong. Ali is old. He was there before the cross. He was there before the prayer. He was there before the mountains had names.

The shepherds of Svaneti do not go above the tree line alone. They go in groups. They carry crosses. They chant prayers. They know Ali is watching from the peaks.

Ali watches. The shepherds pray. The mountains stand between them.
moral: The mountains belong to things older than faith.

title: Kaji, the Fire Spirit
summary: A spirit of fire and lightning that inhabits the hearth, protecting the home when respected and burning it when angered, because in Georgia fire is both hearth and hell.
full_text:
Kaji is the fire spirit. He lives in the hearth. He lives in the flame. He is the warmth of the house. He is the light of the kitchen. He is the fire that cooks the food.

Kaji is not evil. He is not good. He is fire. Fire does not distinguish between the meal and the house. Fire burns what it touches.

Kaji protects the home. If the family respects Kaji, if they keep the hearth clean, if they do not speak ill in the kitchen, if they offer Kaji bread and salt, Kaji protects. Kaji keeps the cold away. Kaji keeps the evil spirits away. Kaji keeps the house warm.

But if the family disrespects Kaji, if they let the hearth go cold, if they argue in the kitchen, if they spill food on the fire, Kaji burns. Kaji burns the food. Kaji burns the house. Kaji burns the family.

Kaji is also the spirit of lightning. When lightning strikes a house, that is Kaji. Kaji is punishing the family. Kaji is angry. The family must make amends. The family must offer Kaji more bread. The family must keep the hearth burning.

The people of Tbilisi keep their hearths clean. They do not argue in the kitchen. They offer Kaji bread and salt every morning. They keep the fire burning day and night.

Kaji is content. The house is warm. The family is safe.

But there are houses where the hearth is cold. There are houses where Kaji is angry. You can tell by the smell. The smell of smoke. The smell of burning. The smell of a house that did not respect its fire.

Kaji burns. The house burns. The fire does not distinguish.
moral: Fire is both hearth and hell. Treat it accordingly.
source: Georgian domestic folklore, documented by Ilia Chavchavadze

title: Devi, the Mountain Giant
summary: A race of giants who once ruled the mountains of Georgia before humans drove them into the deep caves, where they still wait to reclaim the surface.
full_text:
The Devi are giants. They are as tall as the mountains. They are as old as the rocks. They were there before the humans. They were there before the trees. They were there before the rivers carved the valleys.

The Devi ruled the surface of Georgia. They walked the mountains. They ate the animals. They drank from the rivers. They slept in the caves.

Then the humans came. The humans were small. The humans were weak. But the humans had fire. The humans had iron. The humans had God.

The humans fought the Devi. The war lasted generations. The humans burned the Devi's caves. The humans drove the Devi underground. The humans built churches on the Devi's dens.

The Devi retreated. They went deep. They went where the fire of humans could not reach. They went where the crosses could not burn them.

But the Devi did not die. The Devi wait. They wait in the deep caves. They wait in the caverns beneath the mountains. They wait for the humans to forget. They wait for the fires to go out. They wait for the crosses to crumble.

When the humans forget, the Devi will return. They will climb from the caves. They will reclaim the mountains. They will walk the surface again.

The people of Khevi say the Devi are still in the caves. They say the earthquakes are the Devi moving. They say the storms are the Devi angry. They say the avalanches are the Devi pushing against the mountains.

The people of Khevi do not enter caves alone. They do not dig too deep. They do not forget.

The Devi wait.
moral: The earth remembers who was here first, and it is patient.

title: Dze-temi, the Night Hunter
summary: A spectral hunter who rides through the night sky, chasing the souls of the dead, because in Georgia the hunt never ends.
full_text:
Dze-temi rides at night. He rides a black horse. The horse has no eyes. The horse has no rider. Dze-temi is the rider. Dze-temi is the horse. They are one.

Dze-temi hunts souls. The souls of the dead who have not crossed over. The souls who are trapped between worlds. The souls who are afraid.

Dze-temi chases them through the sky. He rides across the mountains. He rides across the valleys. He rides across the rivers. The souls run. Dze-temi follows.

When Dze-temi catches a soul, he takes it. He takes it to the underworld. He delivers it to Al. The soul is gone. The soul is underground. The soul will never return.

Dze-temi appears on nights when the moon is dark. He appears as a shadow on the horizon. He appears as a sound like hooves on stone. He appears as a wind that smells of earth and iron.

The people of Kakheti do not walk at night when the moon is dark. They stay inside. They lock the doors. They light candles. They pray.

They know Dze-temi is riding. They know the souls are running. They know the hunt is on.

Some people have seen Dze-temi. They have seen the black horse on the ridge. They have seen the shadow against the sky. They have heard the hooves. They have felt the wind.

They do not speak of it. To speak of Dze-temi is to invite Dze-temi. To speak of the hunt is to join the hunt.

The people of Kakheti keep their silence. The souls run. Dze-temi rides. The night is long.
moral: The hunt for souls never ends, and the night belongs to the hunter.

title: Dzudzerume, the Mountain Witch
summary: A mountain witch who steals children and replaces them with changelings, because in Georgia the mountains take what they want.
full_text:
Dzudzerume lives in the mountains. She is old. She is older than the trees. She is older than the rivers. She is as old as the rocks.

Dzudzerume wants children. She cannot have children of her own. She is too old. She is too stone. So she takes them.

Dzudzerume appears at night. She appears as a beautiful woman. She appears at the window. She sings to the child. The child sleeps. The child dreams of mountains. The child dreams of snow. The child dreams of a woman with stone hands.

In the morning, the child is changed. The child is quiet. The child does not cry. The child does not laugh. The child stares. The child's eyes are different. The child's eyes are old.

The mother knows. The mother has been warned. The mother checks the child. The child is not her child. The child is a changeling. The child is a stone child. The child is what Dzudzerume left behind.

The only way to get the real child back is to find Dzudzerume. You must go to the mountains. You must find her den. You must take the child back. Dzudzerume will not give the child willingly. You must trick her. You must outsmart her.

Some mothers find their children. Some mothers do not. Some mothers search the mountains forever. Some mothers never return.

The people of Tusheti name their children early. They name them before Dzudzerume can take them. They keep the names close. They whisper the names at night. The names protect the children.

Dzudzerume listens. She waits. She knows the names too.

The mountains are patient. Dzudzerume is patient. The children are not safe.
moral: The mountains take what they want, and they leave something behind.

title: The Xan of Mountain Passes
summary: A shepherd encounters a Xan, a restless mountain ghost, and learns why the dead sometimes refuse to leave the high places they loved in life.
full_text:
In the rugged passes of the Greater Caucasus, where mist clings to the stones like mourning cloth, there lived a shepherd named Orkhan. He tended his flocks along ridges so narrow that a single misstep would send a man tumbling into the valley below. The old women of his village warned him never to whistle after sunset, for whistling called the Xan.

The Xan were ghosts of those who had died in the mountains. Herders crushed by avalanches, warriors slain in border skirmishes, wanderers lost to the winter cold. Their spirits could not rest because the mountains had claimed them too suddenly, too violently. So they lingered, drifting through the passes like fog, their forms flickering between the living and the gone.

Orkhan had never believed. He was a practical man, more concerned with the weight of his cheese bundles than the weight of old superstitions. But one autumn evening, as he drove his flock down from the high meadow, the temperature dropped with unnatural speed. The goats bleated in panic and huddled together. A figure appeared on the trail ahead, standing where no man could stand on such a narrow ledge.

It wore the clothes of a herder from three generations past. Its face was not cruel, but it carried an expression of profound confusion, as though it had been walking for a very long time and could not remember why. The Xan looked at Orkhan with hollow eyes and spoke, though its voice sounded like wind through a crevice: 'Do you know the way down? I have forgotten the way down.'

Orkhan's first instinct was to run, but something in the ghost's sorrow held him. He thought of his own grandfather, who had vanished in a blizzard twenty years ago and whose body was never found. Perhaps this was one of the lost ones, trapped between the peak and the valley, between death and memory.

He took off his woolen scarf and held it out. The Xan reached for it, and where its fingers touched the fabric, the wool grew ice-cold but did not tear. Orkhan tied one end to a rock and laid the scarf along the path, a thread of warmth marking the way downward. He walked ahead, and the Xan followed, step by careful step, its bare feet leaving no prints in the dust.

When they reached the tree line, where the mountain gives way to forest and the living world begins again, the Xan paused. The confusion had left its face, replaced by something like gratitude. It touched Orkhan's shoulder, and the cold was so deep it burned, but only for a moment. Then the ghost walked into the trees and did not return.

Orkhan retrieved his scarf the next morning. It was whole but stiff with frost that would never melt. He kept it hanging above his hearth for the rest of his days, a reminder that the mountains hold their dead close, and that the dead sometimes need a gentle hand to guide them home.

From that day, he never mocked the old women's warnings. He taught his own children to leave a scarf or a ribbon tied to a stone at the mountain's edge, a small offering for those who wandered the passes. And when the autumn winds blew cold and strange through the village, the people would say that the Xan were walking again, searching for the way down.
moral: The dead deserve compassion, not fear. A small act of kindness can release a sorrow that has lasted generations.

title: Shahmaran, Queen of Serpents
summary: A young man discovers Shahmaran, the serpent queen who rules a hidden kingdom beneath the earth, and must choose between the world above and the world below.
full_text:
There was a time when the caves beneath the Talysh Mountains held a kingdom unlike any other. Its walls were veined with minerals that glowed like captured starlight, and its halls were ruled by Shahmaran, the Queen of Serpents. She had the body of a great serpent from the waist down and the form of a beautiful woman above, her hair dark as obsidian, her eyes ancient as the stone around her.

Shahmaran's domain was called the Serpent Court, and in it lived thousands of serpents of every kind. They were not ordinary creatures. Each carried the wisdom of the earth itself, remembering every age, every empire, every secret that had been buried. Shahmaran was their keeper, and she guarded the balance between the surface world and the deep.

A young man named Tural was digging a well when his shovel broke through into a cavern he had not expected. He fell through the opening and tumbled into Shahmaran's hall, landing at the foot of her throne of living stone. The serpents coiled around him, their tongues tasting his fear, but Shahmaran raised a hand and they went still.

'You have entered my kingdom uninvited,' she said, 'but not undesired. I have watched you for many seasons, Tural. You are honest in a world that rewards deceit, and patient in a world that celebrates haste. I would have you stay.'

Tural was terrified, but Shahmaran was not cruel. She gave him food that tasted of honey and minerals, water so pure it made him weep, and a bed of soft moss warmer than any blanket. For seven days he lived in her court, and she told him the secrets of the deep earth: where the veins of copper ran, where underground rivers surfaced, where the bones of ancient beasts lay preserved in crystal.

On the seventh day, Tural told her he must return. His mother was above, aging and alone, and she would think him dead. Shahmaran's expression did not change, but something shifted in her ancient eyes. 'If you leave,' she said, 'you will forget everything you have learned here. The earth's secrets cannot walk on the surface. And you must never tell anyone where I dwell, for men would come with pickaxes and fire, and my kingdom would be destroyed.'

Tural promised. Shahmaran guided him back to the surface, and the opening sealed behind him as though it had never existed. He climbed the hill to his village and found that only three days had passed, not seven. His mother was alive and well, tending the garden. But when he tried to recall the details of the underground kingdom, they slipped from his mind like water through his fingers.

All that remained was the knowledge of where to dig. He found water where Shahmaran had told him, and his well was the finest in the village. The other villagers marveled, but Tural said nothing of serpents or queens. He lived his days as an honest man, patient and kind, and sometimes, when he pressed his ear to the well shaft, he heard the faintest whisper of scales on stone, as though Shahmaran was listening too.

The people of the Talysh region still tell this tale. They say that if you dig honestly and with respect for the earth, the earth will give you what you need. But if you dig with greed, seeking only to take, the serpents will mislead your path, and you will find only dust.
moral: True wisdom comes to those who seek with honest hearts, and the greatest treasures are those shared freely, not taken by force.

title: The Simurgh and the Burning Garden
summary: The great Simurgh descends from Mount Qaf to heal a garden scorched by divine fire, teaching a village the difference between destruction and renewal.
full_text:
At the summit of the world, where the peaks of Mount Qaf pierce the dome of the sky, the Simurgh nested in an ancient cedar whose roots drank from the rivers of paradise. She was vast and radiant, her plumage a cascade of gold and crimson and the deep blue of twilight. Her wingspan could shadow a city, and her cry could wake the dead or lull the dying into peace.

Far below, in a valley cradled by lesser mountains, there had once been a garden so beautiful that travelers crossed continents to see it. Fruit trees lined its paths, fountains sang in its center, and herbs grew there that could cure any ailment known to humankind. The garden was tended by a woman named Leyla, whose family had guarded it for eleven generations.

Then the fire came. It was not ordinary fire but divine wrath, kindled when the villagers forgot the old prayers and began to quarrel over the garden's bounty. The sky cracked, and a bolt of flame fell like a judgment. The fountains boiled dry, the trees blackened, and the medicinal herbs turned to ash. Leyla stood in the ruin of everything her ancestors had built and wept so bitterly that her tears reached the ears of the Simurgh on Mount Qaf.

The great bird descended. She came not as a storm or a terror but as a healing presence, her wings folding like curtains of light around the scorched garden. The villagers, who had fled in terror, watched from the ridgeline as the Simurgh walked among the blackened trees. Where her feet touched the earth, green shoots pushed through the ash. Where her breath passed over dead branches, new bark formed, pale and tender.

Leyla approached, though every instinct told her to flee from such a being. The Simurgh turned her great head and regarded the woman with eyes that held the memory of every age. 'The garden was burned because your people forgot that it was a gift, not a right,' she said. 'I have restored it, but hear me: this garden must never again be divided by greed. It belongs to the earth that holds it, not to the hands that tend it.'

Leyla bowed and swore the oath. The Simurgh returned to Mount Qaf, and the garden grew back more lush than before. But now it was different. The fruit trees bore varieties that had not existed before, each one carrying a trace of the divine fire within its sweetness. The fountains ran not with water alone but with a liquid that shimmered like liquid silver. And the herbs grew with a potency that startled the healers, for the Simurgh's touch had amplified what was already there.

The villagers learned their lesson. They divided the garden's produce not among themselves but among all who came, strangers and neighbors alike. They rebuilt the old prayers and spoke them faithfully. And every year, on the anniversary of the burning, they would tie ribbons to the branches of the oldest tree and whisper their gratitude to the sky, where, if you looked carefully, you might see a distant glimmer of gold and crimson wings.

Some say the Simurgh still watches from Mount Qaf, waiting to see if the people will remember. Others say she has moved on, her attention drawn to newer griefs and newer gardens. But the garden endures, and in its deepest grove, there is a tree whose bark bears the imprint of a great bird's foot, a mark that no axe can cut and no fire can char.
moral: Destruction is not the end but a reckoning. What is restored with grace must be protected with humility.

title: The Peri and the Poet
summary: A grieving poet is visited by a Peri, a celestial spirit of Persian-Azerbaijani myth, who offers him a choice between forgetting his sorrow and learning its deeper meaning.
full_text:
Nasir was a poet of some renown in the city of Sheki, known for verses so sorrowful that listeners wept before he finished reciting them. His beloved wife Leyla had died in childbearing, and the infant with her. He wrote no new verses, for the only words left in him were the same ones, turning over and over like a wheel stuck in mud.

One night, as he sat in the courtyard of his empty house, a light appeared in the pomegranate tree. It was not flame but something softer, like moonlight condensed into a point. The light took shape, and from it stepped a woman of unearthly beauty. Her wings, when she folded them, were made of something that was not quite feathers and not quite fire.

She was a Peri, one of the fallen angels of Persian tradition, beings of immense power caught between heaven and earth. She had been drawn by Nasir's sorrow, which burned so brightly it had become visible in the spiritual world.

'I have come to offer you a choice,' she said, her voice layered as though several voices spoke at once. 'I can take your grief from you. You will forget her face, her name, the sound of her laughter. You will write again, and your verses will be joyful. Or I can show you why she died, and you will carry that knowledge for the rest of your days.'

Nasir chose the second. Perhaps it was pride, or perhaps he understood instinctively that grief without meaning is merely pain, but grief with meaning is something else entirely.

The Peri touched his forehead, and the world opened. He saw that his wife's death was not random cruelty but part of a pattern so vast he could only perceive its edges. He saw that the child, had it lived, would have brought a plague upon the city, and that Leyla's death had purchased the lives of thousands who would never know her name. He saw that the gods are not merciful in the way mortals understand mercy, but they are just, and their justice sometimes looks like cruelty.

When the vision ended, Nasir was on his knees in the courtyard. The Peri watched him with an expression he could not read. 'Now you know,' she said. 'Will you curse the gods, or will you write?'

He wrote, not that night but the next morning. His new verses were not sorrowful but something beyond sorrow, a luminous grief that acknowledged pain without being consumed by it. People came from across the region to hear them, and said that listening was like standing in a storm and feeling, somehow, that the storm was not trying to destroy you but was showing you how strong you were.

The Peri never returned, but Nasir kept a pomegranate seed in a silver box on his writing desk. He said it was from the tree where she had appeared. The seed never dried, never lost its faint golden glow, as long as he lived.
moral: Grief that is understood becomes wisdom. The deepest sorrow, when it carries meaning, can become the source of humanity's greatest art.

title: The Div and the Fortress of Fire
summary: A Div, a powerful demon of ancient Zoroastrian and Turkic tradition, builds a fortress of black stone to block the sun, and only a fearless blacksmith can challenge it.
full_text:
In the time before the prophets, when the boundary between the mortal realm and the realm of spirits was thin as gossamer, a Div rose from the volcanic vents beneath the Absheron Peninsula. It was ancient, older than the mountains, and its body was wreathed in smoke and embers, its voice the sound of rock splitting in a forge.

The Div hated all light: the sun that burned its skin, the moon, campfires, the light in human eyes when they looked upon one another with love. It sought to extinguish every source, and to that end it began to build. From volcanic rock it pulled stones as large as houses and stacked them without mortar, its bare hands shaping basalt as though it were clay. Night after night it worked, and a wall of absolute darkness rose from the shore to the inland hills, tall enough to cast a shadow over the entire coastal plain. Where it stood, no plant grew, no bird flew.

The people prayed to their gods, but the Div was old enough to exist before those gods were named, and it feared none of them. Wells ran cold. The famous oil springs of Absheron guttered and died. A darkness that was not merely the absence of light but the active presence of its opposite spread across the land.

There was a blacksmith in the village of Khachmaz named Rashad, short and scarred, with hands too large for his body. But he knew fire. He understood something that the priests and warriors did not: that fire is not the opposite of darkness but its conqueror.

Rashad built a fire unlike any he had ever built, feeding it with earth-oil mixed with iron filings and prayers he spoke with conviction. The fire burned white-hot, then blue, then a color with no name. He poured the molten metal into a mold carved from memory: the shape of a great bell.

He carried the bell to the fortress at dawn, when the Div slept in its deepest rest. The wall loomed above him, blotting out the sky. Rashad hung the bell from the highest point he could reach, and with a hammer forged from the same metal, he struck it once.

The sound was deep and resonant, a vibration that passed through stone and flesh alike. The Div woke with a scream that cracked its own fortress walls. The bell rang again and again, and with each stroke the light spread further, eating the darkness like a hunger finally satisfied. The black stones crumbled. The wall fell. And the Div, its power broken, sank back into the volcanic vents from which it had come.

Rashad returned to Khachmaz and hung his hammer above the forge. He never spoke of what he had done, but the oil springs burned brighter than ever after, and the shadows on the coastal plain were ordinary ones once more, the kind that retreat before the dawn. To this day, the blacksmiths of Absheron keep a small bell near their forges, a reminder that the greatest darkness can be undone by a single, well-struck note.
moral: Darkness, no matter how ancient, has a weakness. It is not warriors or priests who defeat it, but those who understand the fire that burns within all things.

title: The Bura of the Deep Waters
summary: Fishermen on the Kura River encounter a Bura, a water demon who demands a price for every fish pulled from the deep pools, and learn that some bargains are best left unmade.
full_text:
The Kura River runs through the heart of Azerbaijan like a vein through a body, and in its deepest pools, where the current slows and the water turns jade-green, the fishermen say the Bura lives. It is not like the gentle water spirits of other lands. The Bura is something older and less forgiving, a demon of the depths who keeps its own accounts.

Three brothers from the village of Shamakhi once cast their nets in the deepest pool, where no one fished because the old men said the water was too deep to measure. Eldar, the eldest, was practical. Kamran, the middle brother, was restless and hungry. Javid, the youngest, listened more than he spoke.

Their nets came up heavy with fish so large and silver they seemed to glow. Eldar wanted to divide them fairly. Kamran wanted to sell them in Baku for a fortune. Javid said nothing, but noticed the water had turned cold and the surface perfectly still.

That night, a voice came from the well in the village square. It was deep and wet, like stones shifting in a riverbed, speaking a tongue from before Turkish or Persian. The Bura had risen. 'You have taken from my pool without asking,' the voice said. 'For every fish you took, a memory will be mine. Not a small memory. A true one. A memory that makes you who you are.'

The brothers were terrified. Eldar felt first: a sudden blankness where the memory of his mother's face had been. Her name remained, her voice remained, but her face was gone, replaced by a smooth, empty space. Kamran forgot the promise he had made to his sweetheart, the one he repeated to himself every night. He woke the next morning content but incomplete, and could not say why. Javid forgot the sound of the river in spring, the particular way it sang when the snow melted. It was a small thing, perhaps, but it was the sound that had shaped his childhood.

The brothers tried to return the fish, but the Bura would not have them. Eldar begged at the well every night, but the Bura only laughed, a sound like bubbles rising through deep water. In the end, Javid remembered something the old men had said: that the Bura was bound by rules older than itself. If it took memories, it could be compelled to return them, but only by someone who offered something of equal value. Not a memory, for the Bura had plenty of those, but a skill. Something learned through years of practice.

Javid went to the well and offered the Bura his skill as a fisherman. He laid down his nets, his knowledge of the river, his ability to read the water and know where the fish would be. It was the sum of his identity as a working man. The Bura accepted. Javid's memories returned, and his brothers' memories with them. But Javid could no longer fish. He could not read the water, could not cast a net, could not tell a trout from a carp.

He became a teacher instead, and taught the children of Shamakhi not to fish in the deep pools, and not to take what they have not earned. The Bura was never heard from again. Some say it sank back into the deepest pool and sleeps there still, waiting for the next fisherman who takes too much. And Javid, who lived to a great age, would sometimes stand at the river's edge and listen, though he could no longer hear what the water said.
moral: Everything taken without respect carries a hidden cost. The deepest debts are not paid in coin but in the things that make us who we are.

title: The Al and the Shepherd's Fire
summary: A band of shepherds on the high pastures of Ararat discover that the darkness between their campfires is not empty, and that the Al watches from the space between flames.
full_text:
In the time before the Flood, when the sons of Aram tended their flocks upon Ararat, there lived a shepherd named Torgom who feared nothing. He had wrestled wolves with his bare hands and once drove a leopard from his fold with a burning brand.

But the old women whispered of the Al, and Torgom laughed at them. 'What is an Al?' he asked. 'A shadow that mothers invent to keep children from wandering.' The old women crossed themselves and said nothing.

One autumn evening, when frost silvered the high meadows, Torgom drove his flock to a hollow beneath a basalt outcropping. He built three fires in a ring and settled in to watch the night. The other shepherds slept, but Torgom kept the first vigil.

In the second hour past midnight he noticed the cold. Not the mountain's natural cold, but a cold that crept between the fires like water through cracked earth. The flames did not dim, yet the warmth fled. Torgom peered into the space between the fires.

There, where the light should have met, was a patch of darkness that did not belong. It was not merely the absence of light but a darkness with weight and substance. And within it, two eyes opened.

They burned with a cold, wet light, like marsh-fire in still water, regarding him with ancient intelligence and utter mercylessness. The Al had come.

Torgom reached for his knife, but his hand would not obey him. The Al drifted closer, tall and thin, wrapped in hair like riverweed, its mouth a wound smiling. 'You laugh at the old women,' it whispered, its voice the sound of embers collapsing. 'But they know what you do not. I am the space between every flame. Every fire you build only makes more darkness for me.'

Torgom spoke from desperation, and desperation has its own wisdom. 'Then I will sit in the dark and face you without light.' The Al laughed. 'Fool. If you build no fire, I will come as the cold.'

Yet in the forest beyond, Torgom found something the Al had not predicted. The trees groaned in a wind he could not feel, and in their groaning was a sound that predated fire, predated light, predated even the darkness the Al called home. It was the voice of the earth itself, humming where neither fire nor shadow could reach.

At dawn Torgom told the shepherds to descend to the valley, to the rivers, to places where water spoke louder than shadow. Before leaving, he poured river water over the basalt and prayed to the spirits of the deep earth to hold the Al beneath the rock.

From that day the Armenians honored both fire and water, learning that the Al cannot be defeated by flame, for it feeds upon the shadows flame creates. But it is held at bay by running water, which speaks in a voice older than darkness, and by the deep roots of trees that remember the world before the Al first opened its eyes.
moral: Disbelief does not protect against what is real; only wisdom and respect for the old ways can hold darkness at bay.

title: Shir the Holy Ram
summary: In the ages before the Ark came to rest on Ararat, a sacred ram carried the seeds of all living things through the floodwaters, guided by the light between its horns.
full_text:
Before the Ark ground its belly upon the slopes of Ararat, before the waters withdrew to reveal a world made new, there was Shir. He was not an ordinary ram, though he looked like one from a distance. His fleece was white as the bone of the moon, and between his horns burned a light that was neither flame nor star but something older than both. The priests of the old world called him Sheed, the Luminous One, and they said he had been born from the first ray of sun that ever touched the earth.

When the Flood came and the mountains were swallowed one by one, Shir stood upon the highest ridge of the land that would one day be called Armenia. The waters rose to his knees, then his belly, then his chest. All around him the world drowned. But Shir did not drown. As the water reached his throat, he lowered his great head and breathed in, and the light between his horns blazed so bright that the waters parted around him like a curtain of glass.

Beneath his fleece, woven into the very roots of his wool, were the seeds of every plant that had ever grown upon the earth. Grain and grape, cedar and thorn, the medicinal herbs that healed the sick and the poisonous ones that killed the wicked. All of them slept in the warmth of Shir's body, waiting for the water to recede.

On the third day, Shir came to a place where the water was still and black and deep. From the depths something rose: a great serpent, black as the water itself, with eyes the colour of a sky that has never known sun. It was Vishap, the dragon of the deep, and it had survived the Flood by becoming one with the water. 'The waters are mine,' Vishap hissed. 'Whatever you carry, it belongs to the flood now.'

Shir answered not with words but with light. He lowered his head, and the light between his horns reached into the black water and found the serpent's eyes. Vishap screamed and recoiled into the depths, but it did not flee. It followed Shir for seven days and seven nights along the hidden floor of the world.

On the eighth day the water began to fall. The slopes of Ararat emerged, and Shir climbed toward the resting Ark. When he reached the summit, he shook himself, and the seeds flew from his fleece like snow. Where each seed landed, something grew. In an hour the mountain was green. In a day it bloomed with every flower that had ever existed.

Vishap, seeing this, retreated to the deepest waters, where it remains to this day, coiled in the dark, guarding its resentment. And Shir lay down upon the summit and closed his eyes. The light between his horns flickered and went out, but his body sank into the mountain and became part of it. The Armenians say that when spring comes to Ararat, the first green shoots always grow in the shape of a ram's horns.

To this day the shepherds of Armenia honor Shir. They do not shear the rams that graze upon Ararat's high pastures until the feast of Vardavar, and the first wool they take is burned as an offering. They say that every blade of grass in Armenia grew first from Shir's fleece, and that the light between his horns still sleeps deep in the mountain, waiting for the next great darkness.
themes: the bond between creature and land
moral: The smallest vessel may carry the greatest cargo; what endures the flood is not the strongest but the most faithful to its task.

title: The Dakhanavars of the Mountain Pass
summary: Two vampires haunt a remote mountain pass in Armenia, draining travelers of their blood through their feet, until a clever monk devises a trap of iron and prayer.
full_text:
There was a time when the road between the monastery of Geghard and the village of Garni was the most dangerous path in all of Armenia. Not because of bandits or wolves, but because of the Dakhanavars.

They were two, and they had no names. They had once been men, so the story goes, but they had drunk too deeply of a forbidden spring that flowed beneath the cliff face, a spring the old priests said connected to the underworld. The water changed them. It made them hungry in a way food could never satisfy, and strong in the way dead things are strong, for they did not tire and did not age.

The Dakhanavars did not attack as wolves attack. They were subtle, patient, and above all quiet. When a traveler passed through the gorge, the brothers would descend from the cliff on their bellies, clinging to the rock like lizards, and follow from above. When the traveler sat to rest, they would lower themselves upon him and feed. Not from his throat, as western vampires do, but from his feet. They pierced the soles with needle-thin fangs and drew blood slowly, gently, so that the traveler felt only a deep weariness and cold creeping upward from the ground.

By morning the traveler would be dead, or if the Dakhanavars were not hungry enough to kill, he would rise pale and weak, having lost something essential. The women said they had lost their laughter. The men said they had lost their courage.

Father Hovhannes, the abbot of Geghard, decided the Dakhanavars must be stopped. He studied the old texts and learned they could not cross running water, could not bear the smell of iron, and feared the names of the saints, not because they were holy but because the names were old and had power, and the Dakhanavars were creatures of silence that could not endure sounds they did not understand.

Father Hovhannes gathered twelve monks and gave them iron nails, each inscribed with a saint's name in letters so small only a scribe could read them. They worked through the night, hammering nails into every stone where a traveler might rest. By dawn the gorge was studded with iron.

That evening Father Hovhannes himself walked into the gorge, carrying only a lantern and a book of prayers, and sat upon the largest stone, the one the villagers called the Widow's Rest. He opened his book and began to read.

The brothers came, sliding silently down the cliff face. But when the first touched the stone, the iron screamed, or so it seemed, and the Dakhanavar recoiled as though burned. Father Hovhannes continued reading, and each word was a nail, each sentence a hammer, and the names of the saints rang through the gorge like bells.

The Dakhanavars fled, climbing the cliff in a frenzy, retreating into the deepest crevice in the rock. Father Hovhannes followed on his belly, still reading, until the brothers had burrowed so far into the mountain that no man could follow. He sealed the crevice with a wall of iron-nailed stone and marked it with a cross.

The pass was declared safe. But the monks say that on quiet nights, if you press your ear to the rock near the Widow's Rest, you can hear a faint sound from deep within the mountain, like two voices whispering in a language that has no name. The Dakhanavars have not died. They are merely waiting, patient as they have always been, for the iron to rust and the names to be forgotten.
moral: Evil that is subtle and patient requires a protector who is equally so; brute force will not overcome what whispers.

title: The Dev of the Iron Cave
summary: A giant Dev imprisoned in a cave beneath the Armenian highlands offers a miner riches beyond measure in exchange for his freedom, testing the limits of mortal greed.
full_text:
In the days when the mines of Alaverdi were still young, there was a miner named Grigor who was known throughout the province for two things: his skill with a pickaxe and his refusal to be impressed by anything. His wife said this was bravery. His mother said it was foolishness.

Grigor was digging a new shaft when his pickaxe struck something that was not stone. Instead of the dull thud of iron on rock, there was a ring, clear and deep, like a bell struck in a cathedral. The rock face cracked, and behind it was a cave, and in the cave was a Dev.

It was enormous, filling the cave the way a storm fills a valley. It had a face that was a landscape of ridges and hollows, eyes like burned-out mines and a mouth like a fissure in the earth. Its skin was the colour of raw copper, and its hair was black iron wire.

'Ah,' the Dev said, and its voice was the sound of a thousand tons of rock settling. 'A miner. How fortunate.'

'What do you want?' Grigor asked.

'Gold. I know where the veins run, Grigor. I have listened to the mountain for centuries. There is a lode beneath this cave that would make the mines of Alaverdi look like a child's treasure box. Free me, and I will tell you where it lies.'

Grigor looked at the carved seal stone in the wall behind the Dev. He reached for it, and the Dev's eyes brightened.

But Grigor stopped. He really looked at the creature, and he saw the hunger it hid behind its patience and golden promises. It was not the hunger of a man for gold. It was the hunger of fire for wood, of flood for valley. If freed, it would not reward him. It would consume everything.

'No,' Grigor said.

The Dev's patience collapsed into rage so vast the cave walls cracked. 'You dare refuse me? I will crush you.'

'Perhaps,' Grigor said, his voice steady though his hands shook. 'But I will not free you.'

He ran through the darkness, feeling his way by touch, and the mountain shook around him. He emerged into daylight and told the elders, who sealed the shaft with twelve tons of stone and a prayer.

Grigor never spoke of the gold he had refused. But sometimes late at night he would stare at his hands, trembling. His wife would say, 'You are not afraid.' And he would answer, 'No. I am not afraid. But I am aware. And awareness is a heavier burden than fear.'

The Dev remains in its cave. The priests say it will remain until the mountain crumbles. But the stone holds, and the seal holds, and the prayers of a hundred years have been layered upon the entrance like mortar upon brick. The Dev whispers, and the mountain listens, but it does not answer.
moral: The greatest treasure a man can possess is the wisdom to know when a gift is truly a chain.

title: The Vishap on the Mountain of the Ark
summary: A primordial dragon guards the deepest waters beneath Mount Ararat, dreaming of a second Flood that will return the world to the chaos it once commanded.
full_text:
The Armenians say the world was made twice. The first time, from water, and the water moved according to its own will, and the will of water is chaos. The second time, from earth and light, and the chaos was pushed down beneath the roots of the mountains, where it still churns and dreams.

The Vishap was the first thing the chaos made. It was not a creature born from other creatures, but a shape chaos gave to itself when it wanted to see and be seen. Its scales were the colour of a sky that has never known dawn, and its eyes were older than the mountain, older than the stars.

When the Flood came, the Vishap rose and rejoiced. For a time the world was as it had been: all water, all chaos, all darkness. But the waters receded, the earth emerged, and the Vishap was driven back into the deep.

It has never forgiven the earth.

Beneath Ararat, in a cavern no mine has ever reached, the Vishap waits and dreams. In its dreams the water rises again. The earth sinks. The mountains drown. And the Vishap swims free, master of a world with no form and no law.

The shepherds of Ararat know the Vishap is there. They feel it in the ground's trembling on still nights, in streams that run cold under hot sun, in caves that exhale salt air though the sea is a hundred miles away. They leave offerings at the mountain's base: bowls of milk, dried herbs, clay dragons broken upon the stone to send the Vishap's image back into the earth.

There was a time when a king of Armenia tried to slay the Vishap. He gathered his bravest warriors and miners and led them to the cave where the dragon's breath was strongest. They dug for seven days past copper veins and iron seams, past underground rivers and caverns where blind fish swam in liquid stone.

On the eighth day the Vishap found them. A sound rose from the deepest point, so low it was felt rather than heard, a vibration that turned men's bones to water. The earth opened. The miners screamed and ran, but the king stood his ground.

The Vishap did not emerge. A wind came from the crevice, cold and wet and smelling of the deep sea, and where it touched the king's skin, the skin turned grey and then black and then transparent, showing the bone beneath. The king fled and died three days later, his body cold, his eyes the colour of deep water.

Since that day no one has tried to find the Vishap. The cave has been sealed with stones and prayers. But the Armenians say that as long as there are those who remember Shir the Holy Ram, who carried the seeds of all growing things through the first Flood, the Vishap cannot rise. For Shir left a light in the mountain, buried deeper than the Vishap's cavern, a promise that the world will not be taken by water again. The Vishap dreams of the Flood, but the light of Shir dreams of the spring, and between those dreams the mountain holds, and the earth endures.
themes: the balance between destruction and renewal
moral: The forces of chaos are never truly vanquished, only held in balance by the sacred promises woven into the foundations of the world.
